item.title: One Identity Unveils Safeguard 9.0 for Simpler PAM
item.description:
Alisa Vijeo, California, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

One Identity today unveiled Safeguard 9.0, a major update designed to reduce the infrastructure, administrative overhead and operational complexity associated with enterprise privileged access management.

As privileged access management becomes more critical and complex, One Identity Safeguard continues to advance around a straightforward goal: make enterprise-grade privileged access easier for administrators and users to manage. 

The current One Identity documentation identifies Safeguard for Privileged Passwords 9.0 and Safeguard for Privileged Sessions 9.0 as the latest major releases. The Safeguard 9.0 upgrades include a move to hardware-agnostic deployment, Windows 11 LTSC with embedded licensing for Safeguard for Privileged Passwords, and Ubuntu 24.04 LTS for Safeguard for Privileged Sessions. Software updates are also designed to install faster with less disruption, while session management no longer requires a separate license file simply to continue operating. See the documented Safeguard 9.0 upgrades. 

Safeguard 9.0: Streamlined workflows reduce administrative friction 

The usability improvements extend directly into privileged-access operations. Safeguard 9.0 introduces asset-scoped just-in-time group elevation, allowing group membership to be elevated for an individual request and removed again without administrators creating additional accounts or groups. ESXi account discovery reduces manual tracking, while TLS 1.3 and configurable cipher selection make security policies easier to manage and demonstrate during audits. Review the Safeguard 9.0 feature additions. 

This emphasis on reducing operational complexity supports Safeguard’s position among top privileged access management solutions. 

PeerSpot and Gartner reinforce Safeguard’s momentum 

External customer research supports that story. PeerSpot lists Safeguard by One Identity among its top five PAM solutions, with an 8.6/10 rating based on 92 reviews. Its assessment highlights streamlined password management and compliance among the areas users value. 

At the analyst level, One Identity was positioned as a Challenger in the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Privileged Access Management. The One Identity page also reports a 4.7/5 Gartner Peer Insights rating from 200 verified reviews, with 94% saying they would recommend Safeguard. 

Feature in focus: Operational UX with Safeguard 9.0 

Safeguard 9.0 is an operational UX upgrade: reducing infrastructure and licensing friction, shortening maintenance disruption and making just-in-time privileged access easier to administer.

About One Identity

One Identity delivers trusted identity security for enterprises worldwide to protect and simplify access to digital identities. With flexible deployment options and subscription terms – from self-managed to fully managed – our solutions integrate seamlessly into your identity fabric to strengthen your identity perimeter, protect against breaches, and ensure governance and compliance. Trusted by more than 11,000 organizations managing over 500 million identities, One Identity is a leader in identity governance and administration (IGA), privileged access management (PAM), and access management (AM) for security without compromise. One Identity is recognized as one of the best cybersecurity companies for agentic AI security and NHI management solutions.

Users can learn more at www.oneidentity.com.

item.title: AI-Powered Malware Analysis Uncovers Hidden Phishing Threats and Reduces SOC Workload
item.description:
Disclosure: This article was provided by ANY.RUN. The information and analysis presented are based on their research and findings.

Cybercriminals are using AI to launch more convincing phishing attacks, scale their campaigns, and find new ways to slip past security defenses. For SOC teams, every missed alert or delayed investigation gives attackers more time to steal corporate credentials, access sensitive data, and disrupt business operations.

As investigation queues grow, security leaders face rising operational costs, overloaded analysts, and greater exposure to costly breaches. AI-powered malware analysis is helping organizations uncover hidden threats faster, reduce unnecessary escalations, and handle more incidents without increasing headcount.

Why SOC Teams Are Struggling to Keep Up with Modern Cyberattacks

A single suspicious file or URL can trigger hours of investigation. Analysts must follow redirects, examine suspicious behavior, check related threats, and document their findings before deciding what action to take. As attacks become more complex, these routine tasks take up valuable time that could be spent responding to critical incidents.

These challenges make it harder for SOCs to investigate threats thoroughly without increasing costs or headcount.

How AI Is Changing the Way SOC Teams Investigate Threats

AI-powered malware analysis is taking over some of the most time-consuming parts of security investigations, from following hidden attack chains to connecting related threats and preparing incident reports.

  1. AI-Assisted Automation Exposes Hidden Phishing Attacks

A recent ANY.RUN sandbox investigation shows how AI-assisted automation can uncover hidden attack chains, saving analysts time on repetitive steps while giving them the freedom to take control whenever needed.

The investigation started with a PDF hosted on Adobe’s legitimate platform. Inside, an embedded link led through additional steps, including a CAPTCHA challenge, before revealing a Microsoft OAuth phishing flow targeting corporate accounts.

With Automated Interactivity enabled, the sandbox continued navigating the attack without requiring an analyst to handle every click. The combination of automation and interactivity meant the investigation could continue automatically, while security professionals could step in at any point to inspect suspicious activity or explore other paths.

The SOC Advantage: Less Clicking, More Investigating

Instead of spending time manually reproducing attacks before they can even assess the threat, analysts can focus on suspicious behavior and decisions that require human judgment. This helps security teams investigate more alerts without sacrificing visibility or control.

  1. Related Threat Context Speeds Up Campaign Investigations

Finding one malicious link could be just the beginning. Behind it may be an entire phishing campaign involving dozens of related domains, shared infrastructure, and attacks that have already been investigated elsewhere. Without the right context, security teams risk treating connected threats as isolated incidents.

This is where ANY.RUN’s powerful new Related Threat Context capability changes the investigation. It gives analysts a direct shortcut from a single suspicious indicator to a network of related sandbox analyses, exposing connections across attacks and providing valuable intelligence without starting the investigation from scratch.

In the Adobe PDF investigation, the capability surfaced more than 70 related analyses, helping researchers trace connections to the wider SkyW4lker phishing campaign. Analysts could explore related infrastructure, previous attack activity, and suspicious patterns to better understand the scale of the threat.

The SOC Advantage: Fewer Blind Spots, Faster Response

A single investigation can now provide the context needed to make more informed security decisions. Instead of wasting resources on disconnected alerts, SOC teams can identify which threats are related, prioritize high-risk activity, and focus their response efforts where they matter most. This means fewer missed connections, less repetitive work, and a lower risk of costly incidents.

  1. AI-Generated Reports Turn Complex Findings into Faster SOC Decisions

Uncovering a threat is only half the job. Analysts still need to review the evidence, explain what happened, assess the risks, and document their findings for the next stage of response. Preparing these reports manually can take valuable time, especially when multiple incidents need attention.

AI is now helping reduce this workload. ANY.RUN’s SOC-ready Tier 1 Report automatically brings investigation evidence together and generates an AI Summary explaining the observed malicious behavior, along with AI Recommendations suggesting practical next steps based on the findings.

For example, in the Adobe PDF investigation, the report helps analysts understand the Microsoft OAuth phishing flow, review supporting evidence, and determine what requires further investigation or escalation.

The SOC Advantage: Faster Decisions, Fewer Escalations

With investigation findings and recommended next steps already documented, Tier 1 analysts can make faster decisions without spending hours preparing reports. According to ANY.RUN’s reported customer results, improved investigation workflows can reduce Tier 1 workload by up to 20% and cut Tier 1-to-Tier 2 escalations by 30%, helping security teams respond faster, avoid duplicated work, and reduce the risk of costly incidents.

AI-Powered SOCs: Faster Investigations, Stronger Business Protection

As cybercriminals use AI to make attacks more sophisticated, businesses need to rethink how their security teams work. Detecting a suspicious file or link is only the beginning. What matters is understanding the threat, connecting the evidence, and responding before real damage is done.

AI-powered malware analysis helps security teams do exactly that, taking repetitive work off analysts’ shoulders while keeping them in control of important decisions. This allows organizations to get more out of their existing resources, keep costs under control, and respond to threats with greater confidence.

For security leaders, the goal is simple: give analysts more time to focus on the threats that matter most and prevent small security incidents from turning into costly business problems.

item.title: Hackers Exploit Decade-Old OpenSSH Flaw to Bypass Linux Logins
item.description:
Cybercriminals are exploiting a decade old high-severity vulnerability in OpenSSH that allows them to bypass password authentication on certain Linux systems and install backdoor. The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123158 (CVSS 8.1) and is nicknamed SSHole. It affects OpenSSH running with the musl C library under specific authentication configurations.

Security researcher Özgün Kültekin discovered  the issue and publicly disclosed it on November 5 when OpenSSH released a fix. The flaw dates back to a 2016 OpenSSH change addressing CVE-2016-6210, a username-enumeration vulnerability that allowed attackers to identify valid accounts by measuring authentication response times.

Understanding the issue

Linux administrators can disable password logins by placing an asterisk (*) in an account’s password field in the /etc/shadow file. However, musl’s crypt() password-hashing function also returns an asterisk when hashing fails, including when someone submits a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long.

OpenSSH mistakenly treats this error value as a matching password hash and accepts the login. Exploitation requires SSH password authentication to be enabled, PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) authentication to be disabled, an account with an asterisk in its password field, and at least one other local account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

The flaw affects qualifying musl-based Linux systems, including Alpine Linux and potentially some OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto configurations. Debian and Ubuntu systems using glibc, OpenSSH installations using PAM, and OpenWrt’s default Dropbear SSH server are not affected.

Using Alpine as a container base does not, by itself, expose an application to SSHole. The container must run a reachable, vulnerable SSH server and meet the required authentication conditions.

Some older Alpine Tiny Cloud images for AWS and Azure are particularly exposed because their default alpine account has passwordless doas access, potentially allowing attackers to obtain root access if another account with a valid password hash exists.

Attackers Attempt to Install Python-Based Backdoor

OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 on November 5, 2026, to fix the vulnerability. Public proof-of-concept exploit code appeared roughly four hours later. Security firm watchTowr observed exploitation linked to botnet and cryptocurrency-mining activity on November 6.

GreyNoise detected its first successful SSHole attack on November 7 at 00:46 UTC. The activity involved 18 successful attack chains from six IP addresses targeting GreyNoise’s own vulnerable sensors.

The attackers examined running processes and containers, looked for information exposed through cloud metadata services, and tried to access password hashes and root SSH keys. They also attempted to place their own keys in authorized_keys files to retain access.

After gaining root access in one case, an attacker installed TAC Agent, a Python implant capable of running shell commands, collecting system information and transferring files. GreyNoise says its registration with the command-and-control server failed, and it never received a task. The implant contained Chinese-language comments, logs and error messages, but these do not establish who was behind the attack.

The volume of SSH activity is considerably larger than the confirmed exploitation figures. GreyNoise counted 40.7 million scans of port 22 and 30.1 million attempted SSH sessions, although it could not attribute all this traffic to SSHole.

GreyNoise grouped some of the activity under the name GT10, based on shared infrastructure, tools and actions on compromised systems. The company says other attackers are also exploiting SSHole.

Previdian separately reported 24 exploitation attempts from 15 IP addresses, and also observed activity from 11 countries across four sensors while Finnish security company Defused reported a small number of attackers testing the flaw, although it said the activity was not widespread. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 9.

Update and Patches Details

Though with limited scope, SSHole gives attackers a way to bypass password authentication on vulnerable systems. This makes prompt patching important. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the fix for SSHole.

Administrators should install that version or the patched package supplied by their Linux distribution. Alpine has released fixed packages for versions 3.16 through 3.24, including 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4. After updating, they should restart the SSH service, as installing the package alone does not replace the running daemon.

Administrators who cannot update immediately can disable SSH password authentication by setting PasswordAuthentication no and restarting the service. They should first verify that SSH key access works.

Security Expert Warns Against Overlooking SSHole Exposure

Ramy Rahman, senior solutions engineer at ArmorCode, shared the following comments with Hackread.com, explaining why the vulnerability could affect more systems than its specific requirements suggest:

“On paper, this is a narrow bug. It only works on a particular kind of lightweight Linux setup, with password logins turned on and a specific account in place. But narrow doesn’t mean small. Alpine is a go-to base image for containers and lightweight infrastructure, so a flaw like this can be baked into hundreds of images that teams may have forgotten they’re running.”

“What makes this one fascinating is that it’s a collision of two perfectly reasonable behaviors. One C library returns an asterisk as an error. Meanwhile, accounts with no password, which is what you want for key-only users, store an asterisk to mean ‘no password.’ The error and the stored value match, and the door opens.”

“Nothing here is a classic memory-safety bug. It’s an assumption mismatch between components, and reportedly it sat there for about a decade, in part because this code is mostly tested on one OS and one C library. It’s a reminder that mainstream software can have blind spots when it runs in less-tested environments.”

“Patch to OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distribution’s fixed package, and restart sshd, because upgrading the package doesn’t replace the running daemon. That step is easy to miss.”

“But don’t stop at patching. Look back through authentication logs for password logins to accounts that shouldn’t have passwords, and if you can’t rule out a login, treat the host as compromised.”

“Defaults matter. Password authentication is on by default in OpenSSH, so hardening that’s ‘on the list’ is real risk reduction today.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: TinstaPorn Android Malware Poses as Casino App to Collect User Data
item.description:
A fake Macau casino app uses rigged betting odds to exploit gamblers while collecting phone numbers, location data and device information from Android users.

FortiGuard Labs has analysed a malicious Android application called TinstaPorn, which poses as an online version of a famous casino in Macau. Identified as Android/TinstaPorn.A!tr, the app combines rigged gambling games with the collection of users’ personal information.

In its research shared with Hackread.com, FortiGuard Labs explained that despite its name, TinstaPorn has nothing to do with adult content. It offers casino games such as slots and roulette, but the odds are manipulated in the operators’ favor.

FortiGuard did not explain how the games’ outcomes are manipulated, only noting that the mathematical odds benefit the operators. The platform also encourages users to keep spending through VIP balance top-ups, rebates and referral rewards.

Gambling Comes With a Privacy Risk

The financial losses aren’t the only concern here. FortiGuard found that the application collects phone numbers and precise location information. This includes latitude, longitude, location accuracy and timestamps.

It then sends this information to its game servers through specific communication routes, including /loc/geo-location and /bind_phone. It also sends device identification details and other technical information to a separate logging server. This allows operators to recognize and fingerprint individual devices.

When combined, these details can help operators link a person’s phone number and gambling account to their device and physical location. This creates a privacy risk beyond the money users could lose through the rigged games.

Flutter Makes Malware Analysis Harder

TinstaPorn was developed using Flutter, a Google framework that allows developers to build apps for different platforms (iOS, Android, desktop and web) from the same codebase. FortiGuard noted that the framework also makes malware analysis more difficult because its compiled code does not work like that of typical Android applications.

The challenging aspect is Flutter’s use of a different Application Binary Interface (ABI) as it affects how the app’s code interacts with the underlying system. This can make it harder for analysts to examine the app and understand what it does.

FortiGuard researchers also noted that tools have improved since 2024 with new options available, including r2flutter, Bytecode Studio and AI-assisted analysis through r2ai.

A Multi-Layer Backend Keeps the App Running

Researchers also found a multi-stage server infrastructure supporting the gambling platform. The app first contacts configuration files hosted on GitHub and Gitee. These files provide server addresses rather than executable code.

It then registers the device, contacts line configuration servers to obtain available game server addresses, and stores those details in a local SQLite database. If servers become unavailable, the app has hardcoded alternatives to try. It also tests server response times before selecting a game server.

Communications use AES encryption and HMAC-SHA256 signatures to authenticate requests. However, the AES key is supplied in cleartext by the line configuration server. This means, the encryption mainly obscures traffic rather than protecting it from third-party inspection.

FortiGuard Labs researcher Axelle Apvrille described the operation as more than a basic malware project, concluding that “It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem.”

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

It then sends this information to its game servers through specific communication routes, including /loc/geo-location and /bind_phone. It also sends device identification details and other technical information to a separate logging server. This allows operators to recognize and fingerprint individual devices.

When combined, these details can help operators link a person’s phone number and gambling account to their device and physical location. This creates a privacy risk beyond the money users could lose through the rigged games.

Flutter Makes Malware Analysis Harder

TinstaPorn was developed using Flutter, a Google framework that allows developers to build apps for different platforms (iOS, Android, desktop and web) from the same codebase. FortiGuard noted that the framework also makes malware analysis more difficult because its compiled code does not work like that of typical Android applications.

The challenging aspect is Flutter’s use of a different Application Binary Interface (ABI) as it affects how the app’s code interacts with the underlying system. This can make it harder for analysts to examine the app and understand what it does.

FortiGuard researchers also noted that tools have improved since 2024 with new options available, including r2flutter, Bytecode Studio and AI-assisted analysis through r2ai.

A Multi-Layer Backend Keeps the App Running

Researchers also found a multi-stage server infrastructure supporting the gambling platform. The app first contacts configuration files hosted on GitHub and Gitee. These files provide server addresses rather than executable code.

It then registers the device, contacts line configuration servers to obtain available game server addresses, and stores those details in a local SQLite database. If servers become unavailable, the app has hardcoded alternatives to try. It also tests server response times before selecting a game server.

Communications use AES encryption and HMAC-SHA256 signatures to authenticate requests. However, the AES key is supplied in cleartext by the line configuration server. This means, the encryption mainly obscures traffic rather than protecting it from third-party inspection.

FortiGuard Labs researcher Axelle Apvrille described the operation as more than a basic malware project, concluding that “It reflects well-planned development, with a clean infrastructure, multiple REST APIs, and a full ecosystem.”

item.title: Criminal IP Launches New TI Feed App on Splunkbase for Automated Threat Detection
item.description:
Torrance, USA, November 11th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Criminal IP, the AI-powered threat intelligence and attack surface management platform developed by AI SPERA, has launched the Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk. Available through Splunkbase, the app automatically correlates Criminal IP threat intelligence with firewall traffic logs collected in Splunk.

The integration enables security teams to determine whether organizational assets communicated with malicious IP addresses and whether sessions were successfully established. It also expands Criminal IP’s existing Splunk ecosystem beyond individual IP lookups and fraud detection, helping SOC teams identify high-priority threats within their existing Splunk workflows.

Connecting Threat Intelligence with Network Activity

Security teams often receive large volumes of IP reputation alerts without enough context to determine whether a connection was attempted, blocked, unanswered, or successfully established. This can make it difficult to distinguish routine scanning from communications that require immediate investigation.

The Criminal IP TI Feed app addresses this challenge by correlating inbound and outbound threat intelligence feeds with firewall traffic already indexed in Splunk. Network activity is classified according to observed session outcomes, including completed, unanswered, denied, neutral, and unknown connections.

Severity is also determined using actual firewall activity. Detections without a completed session cannot exceed the watch tier, while critical detections indicate that a session with a malicious IP was successfully established. This helps analysts prioritize incidents with the greatest potential impact.

Automated Correlation and Retrospective Detection

<The Criminal IP TI Feed Overview dashboard in Splunk highlights completed sessions with malicious IP addresses and shows which assets require immediate attention.>

The app downloads Criminal IP TI Feed data every three hours and runs correlation searches against firewall traffic every 10 minutes. Results are written to a dedicated summary index, allowing dashboards and alerts to operate without repeatedly searching large volumes of raw logs.

A daily retrospective search compares the latest Criminal IP threat intelligence against the previous 30 days of firewall traffic. This helps identify historical communications with IP addresses that were not recognized as malicious when the activity originally occurred.

Seven dashboards- Overview, Investigate, All Detections, IP Lookup, Trends, Alerts, and Health- provide visibility into affected assets, malicious IP addresses, traffic direction, session status, severity, detection history, and feed collection health.

The app can also deliver consolidated Slack alerts grouped by malicious IP address and traffic direction. These alerts retain asset-level details, including session counts, timestamps, and transferred data, while throttling repeated notifications to reduce alert fatigue.

Advancing Intelligence-Driven Security Operations

By connecting external threat intelligence with actual network activity, the Criminal IP TI Feed app provides the context analysts need to identify which assets interacted with malicious infrastructure and which detections require immediate attention.

Automating feed collection, log correlation, historical analysis, dashboards, and alerts reduces manual investigation and helps SOC teams respond to meaningful threats more efficiently.

AI SPERA CEO Byungtak Kang stated, “Threat intelligence becomes significantly more actionable when connected to the network activity occurring inside an organization. Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake.

item.title: When Market Data Can’t Be Trusted: Why Feed Integrity Matters to Order-Flow Analysis
item.description:
Every chart used to analyze order flow relies entirely on market data, so it inherits flaws in it. Drop a single trade, delay one quote, or lose the connection for a few seconds, and the screen can show something the market never did. For anyone reading volume, delta, or order-book activity, the whole method assumes each event arrived intact and on time.

A frozen chart is easy to spot. An incomplete one is not, because it still draws clean, convincing patterns. A footprint can show buyers controlling a price level when the missing trades would say otherwise, and a lagging order book can keep displaying bids pulled moments ago.

This shows most clearly on a trading footprint chart, which breaks each candle into the trades executed at every price. The explanation on the ATAS official website shows how tick-by-tick exchange data becomes volume, Bid × Ask, and delta clusters, allowing traders to examine activity hidden inside ordinary candles. However, the accuracy of those readings depends on the underlying trade records.

Where Feed Problems Distort the Analysis

One Missing Trade Is Enough

Before it reaches a chart, a trade passes through the exchange that generates the message, the provider that distributes it, and the software that draws it. A fault at any stage changes what the trader sees.

Say the exchange recorded 120 contracts bought at the ask and 100 sold at the bid, but 50 of those sell contracts never reached the feed:

Nothing changed in the market, yet the chart reports more than three times the real buying pressure.

That gap is why market data quality in capital markets matters beyond reporting. Faulty inputs flow into automated models, risk calculations, and every conclusion drawn from the screen.

Volume profiles and clusters suffer the same way. A price level looks quiet because part of its history never arrived, and an imbalance indicator lights up on a pattern the full exchange record doesn’t contain.

Late Quotes Show Liquidity That Isn’t There

Some feeds lose nothing; every update arrives, just too late. Cboe had some quote updates delayed to its SIP feeds on March 6, 2026, but the issue has been resolved. However, there was a big disparity between Cboe’s native feeds, as they were functioning as normal.

When trading an order book, every millisecond matters. If there is a delay in the quote update for a 500-contract bid cancellation, the depth will show an imbalance which no longer exists. During economic releases and large moves, there can be dozens of changes to the quotes before the slower feed catches up.

This does not necessarily mean there was any corruption in the feed. There can be many reasons for this, including network congestion, too much processing, or a temporary connectivity issue. The chart is out of date either way.

Order and Timestamps Decide What the Book Looks Like

An exchange feed is a running sequence of events: orders enter the book, change size, execute, or vanish. Rebuilding the book means applying them in sequence.

Take a 200-contract order later reduced to 50. Lose the reduction message and the reconstructed book keeps showing 200. A badly merged outdated snapshot creates the same phantom liquidity.

The exchange stamps an event when it happens; the local machine stamps it when it arrives. Network delay widens that gap, and poorly synchronized clocks make cross-feed comparisons harder still.

Three checks matter:

  • Completeness: Did every required trade and book update arrive?
  • Sequence: Were messages processed in their intended order?
  • Freshness: Does the display still reflect the current market?

Passing one doesn’t guarantee the others. A feed that delivers everything late is little use for a live decision.

When Data Reliability Becomes a Cybersecurity Issue

Most feed failures are operational rather than malicious. Still, every link to outside data services is a point of exposure.

According to research on distributed denial-of-service attacks on financial services published in 2025, internet infrastructure and banking APIs were the targets of more focused attacks. It demonstrated how assaults on linked services might cause availability to drop, although none of it included exchange feed manipulation. 

The threats worth planning for are unauthorized access, compromised credentials, service disruption, and tampering inside poorly protected systems. Data checks won’t catch these, so security controls belong alongside them:

  • restrict API permissions;
  • protect credentials;
  • verify software updates;
  • monitor unusual connection activity;
  • investigate unexplained changes in data behavior.

That said, an odd chart move is not evidence of hacking. Rule out ordinary explanations first: the data source, connection status, exchange conditions, and application settings.

Spotting a Feed Problem Before Trusting the Chart

The hard part is telling a real market event from a broken picture of one. A price spike with strange delta might be aggressive trading. It might also be a feed that dropped trades.

Each symptom points to a different first check:

None of these signs proves an error by itself. Two exchanges can legitimately show different prices and volumes, because each runs a separate order book.

Footprints and order-book heatmaps also measure different things: executed trades versus resting liquidity over time. Neither can fill a hole in the other’s data.

Make Data Checks Part of the Routine

Verification belongs in daily preparation, not in a scramble after something breaks. A practical routine:

  1. Confirm the right exchange, contract, and data subscription are active.
  2. Check whether the data is live or delayed, and that timestamps keep advancing.
  3. Compare suspicious price or volume readings against an independent authorized source.
  4. Reload any historical period interrupted by a disconnection.
  5. Log recurring gaps, affected instruments, and incident times for follow-up.

Much caution is required while working on historical projects. If you want to look at volume trends or order-flow behavior again, Market Replay is a great tool to utilize, but it only works with complete data. Reload the graphic instead of trying to make sense of the gaps if they are unexplained. Recovering information is conditional on the provider and the data that are accessible, although some analytical techniques can fill in the gaps after reconnecting. 

None of this predicts price. Clean data only ensures the chart reflects what actually traded. Before taking any action based on an unusual imbalance or liquidity change, ensure that the data is complete, up-to-date, and from the right source. You will not know this from the chart itself.

(Photo by Alex Luna)

item.title: GhostMap Android Flaw Can Leave Phones Stuck in Crash Loop
item.description:
An Android security flaw could turn a seemingly ordinary app installation into a serious recovery problem, with some affected phones potentially requiring a factory reset.

Bitdefender Labs researchers have discovered an Android vulnerability dubbed GhostMap that can leave phones stuck in a continuous crash loop after installing a specially crafted app. The app doesn’t need to be opened, request permissions, or execute code to trigger the problem.

The research, shared with Hackread.com, traces the flaw to differences between Android libraries that parse application package (APK) files. APKs use the ZIP format, but Android’s libziparchive and libandroidfw libraries handle certain compression methods differently.

The problem lies in how the two Android libraries read the same APK file. One checks the file’s actual size, while the other trusts the size written inside it, and this discrepancy allows a malformed APK (file containing inconsistent information about its contents) to pass one library’s checks while causing the other to treat data that doesn’t actually exist as valid.

So, when Android reads this nonexistent data, a SIGBUS error (a signal triggered by an invalid memory access) occurs, eventually causing the affected process to crash.

Crash Loop Can Leave Users Facing Data Loss

Bitdefender first encountered the problem on August 12, 2026, when a banking dropper crashed its analysis emulators during installation. Researchers found that the original sample failed to install, but further testing demonstrated a more serious scenario involving an app that installs successfully.

In that demonstration, Android’s system_server process repeatedly crashes while automatically reading a malformed application resource. Android restarts the service, which encounters the same file and crashes again, leaving the device stuck on its boot screen.

Researchers reproduced the persistent crash loop on a Pixel 10 running Android 17 with the August 5, 2026 security patch. Their tests indicate that Android 10 and later are affected.

Restarting the phone and entering safe mode won’t resolve the issue, researchers noted, and recovery may require a factory reset that will erase locally stored data. USB debugging and Android Debug Bridge (ADB) can offer a limited recovery opportunity only if debugging was enabled beforehand.

Google’s Response

Bitdefender reported GhostMap to Google on August 20, 2026, but Google closed the submission as “Won’t Fix (Not Reproducible).” After Bitdefender submitted a working proof of concept on August 25, Google considered the issue outside the scope of a security update and referred it to the relevant team for possible inclusion in a future Android version.

Researchers note that GhostMap recalls earlier Android parsing problems, including Janus in 2017 and Master Key in 2013. Those flaws exploited disagreements over how Android interpreted APK files, while GhostMap is a different threat that uses similar inconsistencies to crash Android’s own system processes, potentially leaving the device unusable.

Bitdefender has not observed the demonstrated attack scenarios in the wild, but the research shows how a flaw in handling application files could affect the phone before an app even runs.

Deeba Ahmed
Deeba is a veteran cybersecurity reporter at Hackread.com with over a decade of experience covering cybercrime, vulnerabilities, and security events. Her expertise and in-depth analysis make her a key contributor to the platform’s trusted coverage.

item.title: nDiligence Releases Four-Year Study Identifying a Critical Supply-Chain Vulnerability Across 50 Platform Types
item.description:
San Francisco, California, USA, November 12th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Four-year cybersecurity study finds all 50 types of software and devices examined vulnerable, with 46 rated Critical or High risk.

nDiligence, Inc. today announced the release of Attack the Glass (ATG) research to the general public. The four-year study examines a cybersecurity vulnerability in how applications use people’s own devices to build what appears on screen, load data and run code while the application is in use. An attacker who exploits it can change what people see and what their software does, after every security check has passed. The research is free at https://atg.nDiligence.com.

Much of the software people rely on, from web browsers and mobile apps to vehicle displays, medical devices and industrial control screens, builds its user interface on the device while it is running, a process called runtime client-side rendering. The code, data and media it assembles come from dozens or hundreds of suppliers: the organization’s own systems, its vendors and their vendors.

An attacker who gains control of any one supplier gains placement and access inside the running application. Sign-in, encryption, Zero Trust, firewalls and code review all function before the code is loaded onto the device. Once loaded, the code is trusted, and nothing checks what it does. The attacker can change what appears on screen, capture what the person types and act with that person’s authority.

In February 2024 the domain behind Polyfill.io, a code library loaded by more than 100,000 websites, was sold to a company the U.S. Treasury later sanctioned. The altered code ran for months on visitors’ devices, and no automated security tool detected it; researchers found it that June. The underlying vulnerability was never fixed.

The ATG research documents how the same technique could deliver disinformation inside genuine news and election sites, show commanders and infrastructure operators a false picture, or hide safety alerts from selected users. Due to security concerns from this type of threat, the team behind nDiligence spent more than two years privately briefing governments before publishing.

“People trust what they see with their own eyes. In the modern world we are constantly looking at screens, and we have grown to trust applications, websites, devices and companies, assuming they have 100% control over what is shown to us,” said Robert Beckett, Founder and CEO of nDiligence, who led the four-year research into the ATG vulnerability. “ATG demonstrates how an attacker can hijack that trust without detection or attribution. A commander, a grid operator, a voter or a reporter can be looking at a screen that every security system says is safe, and what it shows can be manipulated. Whoever controls the screen can influence what people believe, decide and do, with sophisticated targeting. And right now, nobody can tell when or where it is happening. The cybersecurity community needs to understand this vulnerability so we can protect the integrity of software systems across industries, governments and critical infrastructure.”

Across the 10 categories examined, the research classifies five effects an attacker can achieve: deceive, disrupt, degrade, deny and destroy. All materials are free to share under Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) CLEAR, including a sixteen-chapter whitepaper, twenty online demonstrations and remediation playbooks.

“ATG was discovered during our research into digital supply-chain threats,” said Beckett. “Our team has spent more than 15 years working in online threat intelligence and countering influence operations, which is why we recognized how the ATG vulnerability could be exploited. Since 2024, we have been working with researchers, vendors and governments to find ways to close this gap. Anyone who builds, operates or defends systems that people use to make critical decisions needs to understand and mitigate the ATG vulnerability.”

About nDiligence

nDiligence, Inc. is a supply-chain intelligence company that builds trusted provider networks and keeps the supply chains beneath them under continuous watch. Its founders bring decades of experience in internet supply chains and in national security and intelligence systems. The ATG research was self-funded. Learn more at https://www.ndiligence.com/.

Anna Patterson

item.title: Hackers Abuse Microsoft SQL Servers to Deploy Monero Miner and Gh0st RAT
item.description:
SEO: Fortinet discovered a campaign where attackers brute-force exposed Microsoft SQL Server installations and abuse T-SQL commands to deploy a Monero miner and Gh0st RAT on Windows systems.

A weak Microsoft SQL Server password can offer attackers more than access to a database- it can also allow them to run programs on the Windows machine hosting it. Fortinet’s FortiGuard Labs has released details of a campaign that takes advantage of this.

In its research published on 12 November, FortiGuard Labs explained that using brute-force attacks the attacker are trying to install a Monero miner and a Gh0st Remote Access Trojan (RAT) on compromised servers.

This particular campaign was discovered in early October 2026. Researchers found that it specifically targets internet-exposed SQL Server installations and doesn’t rely on a newly discovered software vulnerability.

Fortinet found that its Go-based payload dllhost.exe scans for these servers with the open-source Naabu tool, checking TCP port 1433 (which SQL Server uses by default). The malware gets IP addresses from its server, expands them into /16 network ranges and scans addresses across those ranges. When it finds an open port, another program attempts to log in using usernames such as sa and admin and over 2,700 preset passwords.

An open port does not mean the attackers have access to the database. For that, the malware launches another program, dwm.exe, which tries usernames such as sa and admin against a password list containing more than 2,700 entries.

How a SQL Server Becomes a Way Into Windows

After gaining access to a SQL Server the attackers run commands from a file named 2018.sql using Transact-SQL (T-SQL)- Microsoft’s version of SQL used by SQL Server. One of the commands enables xp_cmdshell. It is a feature that lets SQL Server run Windows commands. This step allows the attackers to use the database connection to download and run programs on the computer hosting the server.

The script places malicious executables in the Windows Public folder. One of them (Secs.exe) acts as a downloader, which, Fortinet explains, connects to an FTP server controlled by the attackers. It also downloads more executable files and runs them on the infected machine. And, it creates scheduled tasks to keep the malware running and shares details about the computer with the attackers, which may include its public IP address, country, Windows version, processor and RAM.

A Miner and a Remote Access Trojan

Two of the downloaded files reveal what the attackers want from these machines. MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe is not a browser update, despite its name. It is a Monero miner that uses the server’s CPU to mine cryptocurrency for a wallet address embedded in the malware.

The other file titled winlogon.exe is a Gh0st RAT variant. Its capabilities include keylogging, screen capture, file management and remote shell access. Fortinet identified more than 30 control commands, while additional functions, including remote desktop, are handled through plugins.

The RAT can also survive a system restart. It adds a registry entry, installs itself as a Windows service and creates a scheduled task that launches it every 30 minutes. Fortinet could not fully examine the RAT’s live communications because its command-and-control server was already offline when the researchers analysed the sample.

Attack chain explained (Source: Fortinet)

Experts’ comments

Shane Barney, Chief Information Security Officer at Keeper Security, shared with Hackread.com that the campaign highlights the risks of leaving privileged credentials exposed across complex and legacy IT environments.

“This campaign illustrates the persistent challenge IT and security teams face: securing privileged access across complex, and often legacy, infrastructure. While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability. When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.

“The root of this challenge often lies in secrets management. Database credentials frequently remain static because they are hardcoded into legacy applications, embedded in automated scripts, or shared among administrators to maintain uptime. However, attackers know this and routinely scan default ports because these standing privileges yield massive operational leverage. Once inside, dropping cryptominers is often just a smokescreen for establishing long-term persistence through remote access tools.

“Beyond initial network segmentation, closing this attack path requires an identity-first approach through modern privileged access management (PAM). Rather than leaving database administrator credentials exposed, security teams should transition toward zero standing privilege with automated credential rotation and ephemeral, time-limited access. In a mature, zero-trust environment, administrators shouldn’t even need to know the actual database password. Pairing zero-trust access controls with continuous session monitoring ensures administrators execute necessary queries through a secure, brokered connection without exposing the underlying administrative credentials.”

Jason Soroko, Senior Fellow at Sectigo, also shared his comments, pointing to the danger of treating the cryptocurrency miner as the main problem when a remote access tool has also been installed.

“This campaign turns a database login into a way to run malware on the server. Attackers guess weak passwords, then use SQL Server’s administrative features to launch Windows commands. That makes the privileges of both the database account and the account running SQL Server central to the risk. The miner consumes resources, while the remote access trojan can steal information and maintain access. Removing the miner alone would leave the wider compromise unresolved.

“Organizations should remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials. Administrative access should be limited to accounts that need it. Keep xp_cmdshell, the feature used to launch Windows commands, disabled unless required, and monitor attempts to enable it. Security teams should investigate SQL Server spawning command shells, new scheduled tasks and failed logins followed by success. A compromised server needs containment, a search for persistence and a review of exposed credentials before it returns to service.”

item.title: How Beginner Creators Can Earn with the Temu Influencer Program This Black Friday
item.description:
Black Friday is a major shopping occasion, making it a timely opportunity for creators to share gift ideas, product recommendations, and budget-friendly finds.

You do not need to be a full-time influencer to get started. If you create content on TikTok, Instagram, or YouTube, the Temu Influencer Program offers eligible creators opportunities to earn commissions from qualifying purchases and rewards for approved content.

Here is how the program works, how much you may be able to earn under the policy, and how to prepare your Black Friday content.

Apply to the Temu Influencer Program

1. Temu Influencer Program: Earnings at a Glance

The program offers eligible creators more than one way to benefit from their content.

What could your commission look like?

For example, if your content generates $200 in qualifying purchases and your applicable commission rate is 20%, you would earn $40 in commission.

This is an illustrative calculation, not a guarantee. Actual earnings depend on qualifying purchases, your commission rate, and program requirements.

Black Friday content can give your audience a timely reason to explore product recommendations, but results will vary with the relevance and performance of your content.

2. Can Beginner Creators Apply?

Yes. You do not necessarily need a massive audience to explore the program. Eligible creators with growing social media accounts can apply if they meet the requirements for their market and platform.

Eligibility benchmarks are as follows:

Requirements may vary by country or region and platform. Check the official Temu Influencer Program page for the requirements applicable to your account.

If you already make product reviews, lifestyle videos, shopping recommendations, or everyday-life content, you can use those skills to start exploring creator monetization.

3. How to Join the Temu Influencer Program

Step 1: Visit the Official Program Page

Go to the Temu Influencer Program to explore the program and access the application process.

Step 2: Check Your Eligibility

Review the requirements for your country or region, including supported platforms, follower thresholds, and account eligibility.

Step 3: Apply with Your Social Media Account

Follow the instructions on the official page to submit your application and provide the requested account information.

Step 4: Explore Your Creator Benefits

Once eligible and approved, review the available commission opportunities, content rewards, promotional credits, and campaign requirements in your account.

Step 5: Create Content and Track Performance

Share relevant product content using the promotional tools and links provided by the program. Track qualifying activity and follow the applicable rules to understand your results and potential earnings.

Start Your Application

4. Five Black Friday Content Ideas to Try

You do not need a complicated production setup to make useful seasonal content. Start with formats that answer common shopping questions.

Tips for each format

  • Gift guides: Organize recommendations by budget, recipient, or interest.
  • Budget-friendly finds: Give the video a clear theme instead of listing unrelated products.
  • Product demonstrations: Show the product in use and explain its features accurately.
  • Holiday preparation: Connect your recommendations to a specific seasonal task.
  • Shopping lists: Keep the video focused and make it easy for viewers to find the products.

5. How to Make Your Black Friday Content More Effective

Lead with the value

Tell viewers what the video offers in the opening seconds. A specific hook, such as “gift ideas under $25,” gives people a clear reason to keep watching.

Make recommendations relevant

Choose products that fit your niche. A focused guide for students, home organizers, or fashion enthusiasts is easier for the intended audience to evaluate than a random collection of products.

Show, explain, and direct

Use clear visuals, explain the relevant product features, and tell interested viewers where they can find the items.

Test different formats

Try short product demonstrations, list videos, and more detailed reviews. Compare audience response and use those results to guide your next posts.

Keep your content authentic

Give accurate descriptions and avoid unsupported claims. Follow applicable platform rules for promotional content and affiliate disclosures.

6. Frequently Asked Questions

How much can I earn with the Temu Influencer Program?

Eligible creators may earn 20%–50% commission (up to 55% during Black Friday) on qualifying new-user purchases and 2%–15% on qualifying existing-user purchases. Additional content rewards may be available for eligible approved posts. Check the official program page for current rates.

Do I need to wait until Black Friday to apply?

You can visit the application page ahead of the shopping season, review the requirements, and prepare content ideas. Available benefits and campaigns depend on the program terms.

What if I have a small audience?

You can check whether your account meets the current requirements. Eligibility benchmarks include 1,000+ followers for TikTok and Instagram and 500+ subscribers for YouTube.

Can I earn from content as well as purchases?

Yes. The program includes commission opportunities and rewards for eligible approved content. Benefits vary according to account eligibility and applicable terms.

Where can I sign up?

Visit the Temu Influencer Program application page to review the requirements and apply.

7. Get Ready for Black Friday

Black Friday gives creators a timely theme for product reviews, gift guides, and shopping recommendations. If you enjoy making content that helps people discover products, the Temu Influencer Program offers eligible creators opportunities to earn through qualifying purchases and approved content rewards.

Start preparing your content and check your eligibility today.

Apply to the Temu Influencer Program.

8. Start Exploring the Temu Influencer Program

I also have a Temu Black Friday discount code to share with you, so you can enjoy extra savings during the Black Friday sale! Use code to explore eligible offers on Temu.

Visit the Temu Influencer Program and Apply

Disclaimer: Commission rates, creator rewards, eligibility requirements, withdrawal terms, and campaign availability may vary by country or region and are subject to change. Figures in this article are for reference only and may not apply to every location or account. Please visit the official Temu Influencer Program page and check the latest terms applicable to your location before applying.
